stories.headline: Update: Iran's New Supreme Leader Vows Revenge Is 'Certain' as Conflict with U.S. Escalates
stories.summary:
Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a formal statement Saturday declaring that revenge for his father's assassination "will most certainly be carried out," marking his first major public pronouncement since taking power. The statement was released following the burial ceremony for former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei, who was killed by U.S. and Israeli air strikes earlier in the conflict. Massive public calls for the death of President Trump were reported throughout the weeklong funeral procession.

Khamenei did not explicitly name Trump in his revenge statement, but Iranian state media and context made the target unambiguous. He had not been seen publicly during the funeral ceremonies, having reportedly been severely injured when the war began. His emergence with a formal vow of retaliation significantly raises the stakes of the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.

The statement coincided with Iran's declaration that the Strait of Hormuz is closed and the IRGC's strike on a commercial vessel, suggesting coordinated escalation across military, political, and naval fronts. U.S. Central Command has responded with new strikes, and the region remains on high alert with no ceasefire currently in force.

Analysts note that the new supreme leader faces significant domestic pressure to demonstrate strength following his father's death, limiting the political space for diplomatic resolution. Western governments and Gulf states are closely monitoring the situation, with multiple U.S.-allied nations in the region having already been struck by Iranian forces in recent days.

stories.headline: Two Killed, Four Wounded in Shooting at Toronto Salsa Festival
stories.summary:
At least two people were killed and four others wounded when a shooter opened fire at the annual Salsa on St. Clair Latin festival in Toronto on Friday evening. Police responded to reports of an active shooter on St. Clair Avenue at approximately 8:12 p.m. local time and found six victims with gunshot wounds; two were pronounced dead at the scene. The festival, in its 22nd year, was being held along a stretch of midtown Toronto lined with shops and restaurants.

Police secured the scene but urged the public to avoid the area as a large police presence remained. As of initial reports, no suspect had been apprehended. Ontario Premier Doug Ford condemned the "senseless violence" in a statement, saying the person responsible "must be caught, brought to justice and spend the rest of their life behind bars."

The shooting is one of the deadliest mass casualty events at a public festival in Canada in recent years and drew immediate political attention at the provincial level. Authorities have not publicly identified suspects or established a motive.

stories.headline: Argentina Forced to Extra Time by 10-Man Switzerland in World Cup Quarter-Final
stories.summary:
Defending World Cup champions Argentina were taken to extra time by Switzerland in a quarter-final match held in Kansas City, with the score level after 90 minutes. Argentina took an early lead through Alexis Mac Allister's header off a Lionel Messi corner, but Switzerland equalized through Dan Ndoye, who finished from a tight angle to draw level. Switzerland were then reduced to 10 men after Breel Embolo received a second yellow card for simulation following a VAR review that reversed the referee's initial call.

The match is one of the most high-profile fixtures of the 2026 World Cup, with Messi leading the reigning champions against a Switzerland side that has consistently outperformed expectations at international tournaments, having eliminated France at Euro 2020 and Italy at Euro 2024. Switzerland entered the match without midfielder Johan Manzambi, who had scored three goals in the tournament before being ruled out with a knee injury.

The result set up a dramatic extra-time period with Argentina holding a numerical advantage but Switzerland still in contention. The outcome of this match will determine who advances to the semi-finals of the 2026 World Cup, co-hosted by the United States, Canada, and Mexico.

stories.headline: Bahamas Plane Crash Kills All 10 on Board on Nation's Independence Day
stories.summary:
A Cessna 402 operated by Flamingo Air crashed into bushes near San Andros Airport in the Bahamas on Friday, killing all 10 people aboard — nine passengers and the pilot. The aircraft had departed Lynden Pindling International Airport near the capital Nassau on a short domestic flight when it reportedly encountered difficulties before landing. Bahamian authorities initially reported one survivor, but Prime Minister Philip Davis later confirmed that person had also died from injuries.

The crash occurred on the Bahamas' 53rd independence anniversary, casting a shadow over national celebrations. Davis told a media conference: 'Today is a day of celebration but it has become a day of mourning.' The country's Aircraft Accident Investigation Authority has launched an inquiry into the cause.

The Ministry of Aviation announced it was temporarily suspending Flamingo Air's air operator certificate as a precautionary safety measure, though officials clarified the suspension should not be interpreted as a finding of wrongdoing by the airline. The ministry also noted a separate safety incident earlier the same day in which another Flamingo Air flight returned to Nassau after the pilot reported a mechanical issue, and a fire subsequently broke out on board after passengers had disembarked.

The identities and nationalities of those aboard the fatal flight have not yet been released. Flamingo Air said it was gathering details and cooperating with authorities.

stories.headline: Nigerian Army Frees All 44 Kidnapped Pupils and Teachers After Two-Month Ordeal
stories.summary:
Nigeria's military announced Friday that it had freed all 44 pupils and teachers abducted two months ago from three schools in Oyo State in southwestern Nigeria, arresting some of their captors in the process. The victims were taken on May 15 from Baptist Nursery and Primary School, LA Primary School, and Community Grammar School in the Osiire district. Several soldiers died during the rescue operation, according to army spokesman Danjuma Jonah Danjuma.

The freed captives are currently receiving medical treatment at an undisclosed hospital and are expected to return home at a later date. Families described the wait as harrowing. One relative, whose wife is headteacher of one of the targeted schools, told the BBC his family had been particularly distressed after seeing videos released by the captors showing her and other victims.

The kidnapping drew widespread alarm in Nigeria in part because it occurred in the predominantly Christian southwest, whereas mass school abductions have historically been more common in the predominantly Muslim north. The case has renewed calls for full implementation of Nigeria's Safe School Initiative, a program launched more than a decade ago following the internationally publicized Chibok schoolgirls abduction.

A renewed wave of mass kidnappings has struck Nigeria in recent months, and security remains a central issue ahead of the country's 2027 general election. Critics argue the government's security response remains inadequate, while officials say they are stepping up protections around schools and vulnerable communities.

stories.headline: Poland Announces WW2 Genocide Memorial, Deepening Diplomatic Rift With Ukraine
stories.summary:
Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk announced Saturday the creation of a national memorial to the victims of what Poland terms a genocide committed by Ukrainian nationalists during World War Two. Tusk spoke on the anniversary of the Volhynia massacre, in which Poland says approximately 100,000 ethnic Poles were killed by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army between 1943 and 1945. He urged Ukraine to 'embrace this truth' if it hopes to one day join the European Union.

The announcement deepens a diplomatic rift between Warsaw and Kyiv that has grown in recent weeks. Last month, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky was stripped of Poland's highest state honor after he named a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, which many Ukrainians regard as heroes who fought for independence from the Soviet Union and against Nazi Germany. Three former Ukrainian presidents subsequently returned their own Polish state awards in solidarity with Zelensky.

In a video address Saturday, Zelensky said Ukrainian and Polish state representatives participated in joint prayers to commemorate the Volhynia victims, and stressed that both nations now face a common existential threat in Russia. Ukrainian officials have historically disputed Polish characterizations of the wartime events and are wary of the UPA being labeled a perpetrator organization, given its symbolic status in Ukrainian national identity.

The dispute carries practical consequences: Poland's support for Ukraine's NATO and EU aspirations is significant, and the row has complicated bilateral relations at a moment when both countries face continued Russian military pressure. Polish President Karol Nawrocki has stressed the diplomatic tension will not affect Poland's military backing for Ukraine.

stories.headline: Hunter Biden Awarded $1.7 Million in Defamation Case Against Former Overstock CEO
stories.summary:
A federal judge on Friday awarded Hunter Biden $1.7 million in punitive damages in a defamation lawsuit he filed against former Overstock.com CEO Patrick Byrne. Biden sued Byrne in 2023, alleging Byrne falsely claimed in an interview that Biden had sought an $800 million bribe from the Iranian government to lobby his father, then-President Joe Biden, to unfreeze Iranian assets. The ruling was issued by U.S. District Judge Stephen Wilson, a Reagan appointee.

Byrne is a prominent ally of former and current President Donald Trump and a well-known denier of Biden's 2020 presidential election victory who funded efforts to challenge those results. He did not mount a substantive defense against the defamation claims, which contributed to the default judgment against him.

The award represents one of the more significant legal outcomes for Hunter Biden following years of politically charged scrutiny, including his federal convictions on gun and tax charges and the broader investigations into his foreign business dealings. Supporters of the ruling argue it illustrates the legal consequences of spreading demonstrably false claims about public figures; critics of the Biden family have maintained that Hunter Biden's overseas business activities warranted aggressive public scrutiny.

The $1.7 million judgment is in punitive damages, meaning it is intended to punish Byrne for the conduct rather than simply compensate for proven losses. Whether Byrne will pay or contest the award through further legal proceedings was not immediately clear.

stories.headline: Israel Shares Intelligence With U.S. on Alleged Fresh Iranian Plot to Kill Trump
stories.summary:
Israel has shared new intelligence with the United States indicating a fresh Iranian plan to assassinate President Donald Trump, according to the Wall Street Journal. Trump himself publicly acknowledged the threat multiple times during the NATO summit in Turkey this week, saying "I'm on every single one of their lists" and calling Iran's leadership "scum." The Secret Service took notable precautionary measures, routing Trump home on the older Air Force One — which carries more sophisticated antimissile countermeasures — while sending the newer Qatar-donated plane ahead to England as a decoy.

The White House confirmed the aircraft switch, with communications director Steven Cheung describing it as deliberate "misdirection" and insisting the new plane also carries high-level security protocols. U.S. intelligence officials told reporters they were not aware of a specific, actionable threat, but acknowledged heightened concern given the current state of U.S.-Iran hostilities. Iran has harbored ambitions of killing Trump since his 2020 drone strike that killed Quds Force commander Qasem Soleimani, and multiple Iranian-directed plots against Trump and former officials have previously been investigated by the FBI.

The alleged plot comes amid an already acute period of U.S.-Iran tensions, with ongoing military exchanges in the region following the breakdown of ceasefire talks. Iranian demonstrators were photographed at Supreme Leader Khamenei's funeral carrying banners reading "We Will Kill Trump," underscoring the rhetorical and potentially operational hostility. The story is covered by 22 outlets across the political spectrum, making it one of the most widely corroborated stories of the day.

stories.headline: Update: Typhoon Bavi Makes Landfall in China, Nearly 2 Million Evacuated
stories.summary:
Typhoon Bavi struck China's eastern coast on Saturday, making landfall first near Taizhou and again near Wenzhou in Zhejiang province, as authorities evacuated nearly two million people from the storm's projected path. The typhoon, stretching roughly 1,000 kilometers at its widest point, has weakened to a Category 1 storm but still poses severe flooding risks due to the enormous volume of moisture in its rain bands. Schools, workplaces, and outdoor activities have been suspended across Zhejiang, and hundreds of flights and dozens of train services have been cancelled.

Bavi previously killed at least 17 people in landslides in the Philippines before brushing past Taiwan's northern tip, where thousands were evacuated. This is the second major typhoon to strike China within a single week; Typhoon Maysak earlier killed at least 39 people on the mainland and triggered rare tornadoes in Hubei province. Wenzhou, a city of roughly 10 million people, lies close to the storm's track, raising concerns about urban flooding and infrastructure damage.

Chinese authorities described evacuations as precautionary against worst-case scenarios, and state media reported largely orderly departures. The rapid succession of major typhoons striking the same region of East Asia within days of each other is drawing attention from meteorologists, as sustained warm sea-surface temperatures in the western Pacific continue to fuel powerful storm development during what is shaping up to be an exceptionally active typhoon season.

stories.headline: U.S. Congressman Ro Khanna Says Armed Israeli Settlers Detained Him for 90 Minutes in West Bank
stories.summary:
Democratic Representative Ro Khanna of California said he and his staff were detained for approximately 90 minutes on Wednesday by armed Israeli settlers in the occupied West Bank while on a fact-finding visit to the destroyed Palestinian village of Khirbet Zanuta. Khanna said the settlers, armed with M4 rifles, surrounded his van and blocked the road. When Israeli Defense Forces arrived, he said, soldiers sided with the settlers rather than facilitating the release of the American congressional delegation, and his staff appealed to the U.S. Embassy in Jerusalem for assistance before police officers ultimately intervened and allowed the group to leave.

The IDF issued a statement saying troops and police "dispersed the Israeli civilians and allowed the vehicles to continue on their way" after responding to a report that settlers had blocked vehicles in the area. It did not directly address Khanna's characterization that soldiers sided with the settlers. Khanna, who is publicly weighing a 2028 presidential run, described the weapons as "American-made machine guns" and said the settlers had destroyed homes and a school in the village.

The incident is drawing significant media attention across eight outlets, and highlights ongoing tensions over Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank. Supporters of Israeli settlement policy argue that settlers face genuine security threats and that IDF presence is necessary to maintain order; critics, including Khanna, say Israeli forces routinely enable settler violence against Palestinians and foreign observers. The West Bank's roughly 160 Israeli settlements, housing 700,000 people, are considered illegal under international law, a position Israel disputes.

stories.headline: Update: Sole Suspect in Ann Widdecombe Killing Released; Police Reveal She Was Attacked a Day Before Body Found
stories.summary:
British police on Saturday released a 26-year-old man who had been arrested as a suspect in the killing of former Conservative MP and political commentator Ann Widdecombe, saying he was no longer under investigation. Devon and Cornwall Police also disclosed a significant new detail: Widdecombe, 78, was attacked at approximately 12:30 p.m. on Wednesday — a full day before her body was discovered Thursday at her isolated rural home in the village of Haytor on the edge of Dartmoor National Park. Concerns were first raised when she failed to appear for a scheduled television interview Wednesday afternoon.

Police have not released a cause of death, saying only that she sustained "serious injuries." Detectives said they are working at "a significant pace" to identify the killer, and that they do not believe there is any ongoing risk to the public. The investigation is not being treated as an act of terrorism, and authorities said there is no evidence it was politically motivated. Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said a review of party emails found no patterns of targeted abuse directed at Widdecombe.

Widdecombe served in the House of Commons from 1987 to 2010 and was prisons minister under Prime Minister John Major. She later became a familiar media figure through reality television appearances and her association with the Brexit Party and then Reform UK. Her death has prompted calls across British politics for a review of security arrangements for current and former lawmakers, following the murders of serving MPs Jo Cox in 2016 and David Amess in 2021.

stories.headline: U.S. Citizen Humanitarian Worker Tests Positive for Ebola in Congo
stories.summary:
A U.S. citizen employed by a humanitarian organization in the Democratic Republic of Congo has tested positive for the Ebola virus, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention announced Friday. The CDC said it is working with the individual's employer, U.S. agencies, Congolese public health authorities and partners to prevent further transmission and identify close contacts, but provided no further personal details.

The case emerges as Congo's current outbreak — caused by the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment — has been declared the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded on the African continent. As of earlier this week, the Africa CDC reported 1,830 confirmed cases and 648 deaths, with cases also confirmed in neighboring Uganda.

Efforts to contain the outbreak have been complicated by a funding shortfall, attacks on health centers, and active armed conflict in eastern Congo, the epicenter of the outbreak. Clinical trials for a potential treatment launched last week. An earlier American doctor infected in Congo was transferred to Germany for care; a separate Trump administration plan to send exposed Americans to a new facility in Kenya was suspended after a Kenyan court order blocked it.

stories.headline: Update: Apple Sues OpenAI, Former Employees and Jony Ive's io Products Over Trade Secret Theft
stories.summary:
Apple filed a federal lawsuit Friday against OpenAI, two former Apple employees now working at the AI company, and io Products — the design startup founded by longtime Apple executive Jony Ive that OpenAI acquired last year — accusing them of engaging in a "pattern of theft" of Apple's confidential product development information. Apple alleges that at least two long-tenured former employees emailed themselves internal Apple data before departing for OpenAI.

Among those named in the suit are Chang Liu, a senior electrical engineer who spent eight years at Apple, and Tang Yew Tan, a vice president of design for iPhone and Apple Watch who worked at Apple for 24 years and is now OpenAI's chief hardware officer. Apple claims OpenAI also allegedly instructed prospective hires who were still Apple employees to bring "actual parts" as "props" for "show and tell" during job interviews.

OpenAI denied wrongdoing, with spokesman Drew Pusateri telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets," adding the company is reviewing the complaint. Apple says the suit stems from "significant evidence" and accuses OpenAI of exploiting Apple's confidential information to accelerate its own entry into the consumer hardware market. OpenAI is expected to release its first hardware product — a type of AI keyboard — later this month and is preparing to go public.

stories.headline: Missouri Flooding Forces Helicopter Evacuation of 200-Plus Children from Summer Camp
stories.summary:
Heavy rainfall and flash flooding struck parts of southeastern Missouri on Friday, prompting the Army National Guard to use Black Hawk helicopters to evacuate more than 200 children and staff trapped at Camp Taum Sauk in Lesterville after surrounding roads were washed out. The evacuees were flown to a nearby elementary school and reunited with their families.

Separately, approximately 20 people who had taken refuge atop a building at the Bearcat Getaway campground near the Black River — about 85 miles south of St. Louis — were rescued after the structure collapsed under the weight of floodwaters. Three additional people were rescued from trees along the Black River in Reynolds County. A woman in Crawford County remained missing after the house she was in was swept from its foundation.

The affected area received between 6 and 12 inches of rain as thunderstorms stacked in succession. Missouri Governor Mike Kehoe declared a state of emergency and activated state search and rescue teams, saying hundreds of people had been saved from floodwaters, rooftops, trees, and stranded vehicles. The National Weather Service warned that additional overnight rainfall could produce further major flood impacts, and the Black River near Annapolis was forecast to crest at a record level above 28 feet.

stories.headline: Update: ICE Confirms Houston Shooting Victim Was Not the Intended Target, Fueling Calls for Investigation
stories.summary:
U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia, a Democrat whose district includes the Houston neighborhood where the shooting occurred, said Friday that acting ICE Director David Venturella confirmed to her that Lorenzo Salgado Araujo — a Mexican national killed by a federal immigration agent on July 7 — "was not a target" of the operation. Salgado Araujo was a homebuilder who had lived in the United States for more than 35 years, had no criminal record, and was reportedly close to completing the legal residency process.

The Department of Homeland Security, which oversees ICE, said agents had been surveilling a property associated with a target and on the day of the shooting observed a white van with a driver who "resembled the target" and initiated a vehicle stop. DHS says Salgado Araujo rammed an ICE vehicle and that an officer fired in self-defense. Critically, DHS acknowledged that the agents involved had not yet been issued body-worn cameras, which it attributed to a prolonged government shutdown.

Garcia called for an independent investigation, saying, "This is just one more death too many." Mexico has previously threatened to file criminal complaints in U.S. courts over deaths of its nationals in ICE custody. Supporters of the ICE operation argue agents acted within protocol after perceiving a threat, and DHS maintains the officer fired in self-defense. Critics, including civil rights advocates and Democratic lawmakers, say the absence of body camera footage and the confirmation that Salgado Araujo was not the intended target demand accountability and a full independent review.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. Demands Iran Declare Strait of Hormuz Open as Nuclear Deal Conditions Harden
stories.summary:
Senior U.S. officials revealed Friday that any nuclear agreement with Iran will require Tehran to surrender its stockpile of highly enriched uranium, while simultaneously demanding Iran publicly declare that ship traffic in the Strait of Hormuz has been fully restored. Officials described an internal Iranian power struggle, with hardline factions blamed for renewed attacks on commercial vessels that collapsed the ceasefire earlier this week. Secretary of State Rubio spoke by phone with Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan Al Saud to coordinate regional strategy.

U.S. officials said negotiators are making progress with Iranian leadership but warned that hardliners are actively undermining diplomacy. Trump has authorized new strikes on Iran in the meantime and, officials said, will not wait indefinitely for Tehran to unify its position. A senior Iranian diplomat at the United Nations struck a defiant note Friday, telling reporters that control of the strait "rests exclusively with Iran" — though Iran also signaled willingness to return to ceasefire terms.

The standoff represents a significant new development in the U.S.-Iran conflict: the explicit linking of nuclear material surrender to any diplomatic resolution, and the public U.S. demand for an Iranian statement on shipping lanes. Officials noted the highly enriched uranium stockpile is believed to be buried underground following earlier U.S. strikes, and said military options exist to ensure it remains there if no deal is reached.

The Strait of Hormuz is a critical chokepoint through which roughly 20 percent of the world's oil supply passes, and continued instability there has ripple effects on global energy markets and allied economies. The IMF has already cut its 2026 global growth forecast to 3 percent, citing the Iran war energy shock.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Fires Remaining Democratic Election Assistance Commission Members, Drawing Bipartisan Criticism
stories.summary:
President Trump removed the final Democratic members of the Election Assistance Commission on Thursday, leaving the independent, bipartisan agency with no sitting commissioners months before the 2026 midterm elections. The EAC certifies voting systems, distributes election security grants, and provides guidance to state and local election officials. The firings followed the earlier resignation of Republican Commissioner Christy McCormick, completing the hollowing out of the body.

The White House defended the dismissals by citing the Supreme Court's recent ruling in Trump v. Slaughter, which expanded presidential authority to remove commissioners from independent agencies. A White House official said the president retains the right to remove individuals "not totally aligned with the important task of securing America's elections and ensuring every legal vote is counted."

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called the move "a brazen attempt to seize control of our elections before a single vote is cast" and vowed Senate Democrats would fight it. Criticism also came from former Republican Georgia Lt. Gov. Geoff Duncan, who said Trump "wants to eliminate oversight of his administration's oversight." The White House countered that it has been working across agencies to safeguard elections from fraud ahead of the midterms and that the Slaughter ruling provides clear legal authority.

The episode is the latest flashpoint in a broader dispute over election administration. Trump has repeatedly conditioned cooperation on congressional passage of the SAVE America Act, his voter ID legislation, and on Friday separately announced he would withhold his signature from a bipartisan housing bill as protest over the Senate's failure to pass that measure.

stories.headline: Speedboat Capsizes Near Vietnamese Island, Killing 15 Indian Tourists
stories.summary:
A speedboat carrying 32 Indian tourists and four crew members capsized Saturday near Hon May Rut Ngoai island in southern Vietnam's An Thoi Archipelago, killing at least 15 people. The vessel overturned approximately 400 meters from shore in rough sea conditions, with high winds and heavy waves cited as likely causes. Nearby tourist vessels responded quickly, rescuing 21 survivors, though several passengers were found trapped inside the capsized boat.

Vietnamese authorities, led by senior Communist Party official Nguyen Tien Hai, said rescue and emergency medical operations were the immediate priority while the final death and survivor tallies were still being confirmed. The Indian embassy in Hanoi released the full passenger manifest and established telephone hotlines for families of those on board.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi said he was "extremely saddened" by the accident and expressed condolences to families of the victims while praying for the recovery of survivors. The incident drew immediate attention from both governments given the scale of casualties among foreign nationals.

Hon May Rut Ngoai, located roughly 10 kilometers south of Phu Quoc — Vietnam's largest island — is a popular destination for island-hopping boat tours. The accident follows a pattern of maritime incidents in Vietnamese tourist waters; a Ha Long Bay tourist boat capsized in a previous incident, prompting calls for tighter safety regulations.

stories.headline: Update: U.S. and Iran Exchange Intensifying Fire as Ceasefire Frays; Tehran Strikes U.S.-Allied Gulf States
stories.summary:
The United States launched new airstrikes against Iran early Thursday, hitting approximately 90 targets including airport runways and missile launchers, according to U.S. Central Command. Iran retaliated by striking U.S.-allied Gulf states — Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar — with air raid sirens sounding at least three times in Bahrain, home to the U.S. Navy's 5th Fleet headquarters. The escalating exchange threatened an interim ceasefire deal that had been intended to wind down the broader regional conflict.

The new development marks a significant expansion of the conflict beyond Iranian territory, with Tehran now targeting third-country soil hosting American military assets. The strikes occurred simultaneously with the final day of funeral ceremonies for Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who was buried Thursday at the Imam Reza shrine in Mashhad as thousands of mourners dressed in black filled the city.

The attacks on Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar — all of which host U.S. military installations — raise the stakes considerably for American force protection and for Gulf Arab governments that have sought to stay out of direct confrontation. The IMF has already cut its 2026 global growth forecast to 3 percent, citing the energy shock from the ongoing conflict.

This is the latest in a rapidly escalating series of exchanges; earlier coverage noted the U.S. had struck more than 170 Iranian targets in the preceding 48 hours and that President Trump declared the ceasefire "over." The new material development today is Iran's direct strikes on Bahrain, Kuwait, and Qatar, broadening the geographic scope of the war.

stories.headline: Update: Spain Wildfire Death Toll Reaches 12 in Almeria; Dozens Missing as Blaze Continues
stories.summary:
A fast-moving wildfire that erupted late Thursday in Spain's southern Almeria province has killed at least 12 people, making it one of the deadliest wildfires in the country's recorded history. Eight people were injured and 23 remained missing as of Friday morning, with Andalusia's regional leader Juan Manuel Moreno confirming the figures. The fire broke out near the Sierra de Los Filabres mountains and swept through a semi-arid area popular with foreign expatriates.

Several of the victims were found inside burned-out vehicles, apparently killed while attempting to flee. Emergency services chief Antonio Sanz said most of the dead had ignored shelter-in-place instructions and that some tried to escape through a dry riverbed that "turned into a death trap." At least four of the dead were believed to be British nationals, identified because their vehicle had a right-hand steering wheel.

The fire was still burning as of Friday, and soaring temperatures linked to a broader European heat wave were hampering containment efforts. Researchers noted that extreme fire events of this scale are becoming a "new reality" driven by climate change, and Almeria province — a popular holiday destination — faced additional difficulty given its large population of foreign residents unfamiliar with local emergency protocols.

This story was previously noted in earlier coverage; the new development today is the confirmed final death toll of 12 and the ongoing search for 23 missing persons as the fire remained uncontained.

stories.headline: Marine Le Pen Announces 2027 Presidential Bid After Court Lifts Ban; Bardella Sidelined
stories.summary:
Marine Le Pen announced Tuesday she will stand as the National Rally's candidate in France's 2027 presidential election after a Paris appeals court lifted her ban from public office, ending months of uncertainty about the far-right party's electoral strategy. Le Pen had been convicted in a fake jobs scandal and barred from running, but the court ruled she should instead serve a year wearing an electronic tag. The decision came just as her protégé Jordan Bardella had been growing into the role of presumptive candidate.

Le Pen declared that she and Bardella would run together as "a winning ticket," with her as presidential candidate and him as a prospective prime minister — though France's constitutional system does not guarantee that arrangement, as parliamentary elections are not due until 2029. Bardella, 30, had publicly said he would only stand if Le Pen remained legally barred, but observers noted his body language at subsequent campaign events suggested disappointment at being passed over.

The announcement has boosted Le Pen's poll numbers, with National Rally holding a substantial lead ahead of the election. Supporters of the party argue Le Pen's three previous presidential campaigns and name recognition make her a stronger candidate than the relatively inexperienced Bardella. Critics on the left contend that lifting the ban allows a convicted fraudster to seek the nation's highest office.

The outcome has significant implications for Europe: a Le Pen presidency would mark the first hard-right head of state in modern French history and could reshape France's relationships with NATO, the European Union, and Ukraine.

stories.headline: Meta Pulls AI Image Feature After Backlash Over Unauthorized Use of Users' Likenesses
stories.summary:
Meta abruptly removed a newly launched feature of its Muse Image AI tool that had allowed users to generate images based on other people's public Instagram content without their knowledge or consent. The feature, which rolled out Tuesday as part of Meta's first foray into AI image generation, automatically opted in all public-facing Instagram accounts, meaning anyone's photos and likeness could be used as source material without permission. Within days, widespread criticism from privacy advocates, creative industry unions, and ordinary users forced the company to pull it.

Hollywood union SAG-AFTRA called the reversal a "win" and said it had urged its members and all Instagram users to act to protect their likenesses, describing the rollout as an "utter miscalculation of public sentiment." London-based human rights charity Privacy International said the episode was "the latest sign AI companies see people's images and data as raw material to be exploited." Meta acknowledged it had "missed the mark" and said the feature was "no longer available."

Meta said its intent had been to provide a creative tool while giving users control over whether their content could be referenced, but critics noted the opt-in-by-default design undermined that stated goal. The company said further AI features are still planned for WhatsApp, Facebook, and Messenger, and an AI video tool is in development.

The episode illustrates the accelerating tension between AI companies seeking to train and power generative tools using publicly available data and individuals who object to their images and likenesses being used without explicit consent — a debate that is intensifying across the industry as AI-generated imagery becomes more accessible.
